chunks.content: Plants past the dome live in retrofitted IKEA glass cabinets (Fabrikör and Milsbo) and a Barrina LP900 grow cabinet. No humidifier is used anywhere: the plants and the enclosed cabinet hold the humidity on their own at the 65 to 80 percent the grow space runs at. Cabinets are the recommendation for anyone wanting to raise humidity, and they pair naturally with LED light bars mounted inside.
chunks.heading: Cabinets instead of humidifiers

chunks.content: Starting humidity is always 100 percent, either a single pot under its own dome or a tray with a dome. Hold 100 percent for at least a week. After about a week, start opening the vents or lifting the lid slightly and keep stepping the humidity down slowly from there. Both directions of error hurt: stepping down too slowly delays growth because the plant needs airflow and lower humidity to keep acclimating, and stepping down too fast, or never giving 100 percent at the start, kills plantlets.
chunks.heading: Humidity: hold 100 percent for the first week

chunks.content: A varied group of fertilizer products is used here and the brand does not matter. What matters is a 3-1-2 NPK ratio in any multiple: 6-2-4 and 9-3-6 are the same thing. If the fertilizer does not already include calcium and magnesium, add a cal-mag supplement. Dosing depends on the specific brand, so follow that product's label rather than a fixed rule; the standing practice is a light dose with every watering except the flush.
chunks.heading: Fertilizer: any 3-1-2 ratio, plus cal-mag

chunks.content: Several kinds of humidity domes are in use: AC Infinity domes with grow lights built into the lid, and domes from Greenhouse Megastore over 72-cell trays. Any of them work; the dome is what lets the tray hold 100 percent humidity for the first week.
chunks.heading: Domes and trays used here

chunks.content: Every watering carries a light dose of fertilizer, for all plants (tissue-culture plantlets skip it on their second watering), and this produced a large increase in growth. The other levers for a plant that has stalled are more light and a consistent routine.
chunks.heading: Light fertilizing with every watering

chunks.content: Do not rush the up-pot. Wait until the plant is properly root-bound, with lots of roots circling the pot. Alocasia especially like to be tightly bound. Customers often up-pot the moment a plant looks snug, but most of these plants prefer it and do not want their roots disturbed. When you do up-pot, leave the root ball alone even if the roots are circling everywhere; at most loosen the bottom slightly. Breaking the root ball apart damages the fine root hairs, including ones you cannot see, and the plant takes much longer to recover.
chunks.heading: Up-potting: wait for root-bound, do not disturb the roots

chunks.content: Nutrient lockout mostly shows up as slower growth. Sometimes there is visible salt buildup on the leaves. To avoid it, one out of every four or five waterings is a heavy top watering with plain water only, no fertilizer, to flush accumulated salts out of the pot. There is no set amount of water per pot; pour until the pot has been thoroughly flushed and drains.
chunks.heading: Nutrient lockout: what it looks like and how to avoid it

chunks.content: When plantlets arrive, do not open the bag. Let them sit sealed for a day or two in the spot where they will be grown, so they adjust to that room's temperature and light before anything else changes.

chunks.content: First: overdoing the start. Distilled water, extra coatings, hormones, and fertilizer on top of each other are not needed, and success rates were higher cleaning the plantlets off under plain running water at the sink. Second: mistiming the humidity step-down, either dragging it out (delayed growth, the plant needs airflow) or yanking the dome off or never starting at 100 percent (kills the plant). Third: potting into a soil that is too dense.
chunks.heading: Mistakes beginners make most

chunks.content: For the first watering, per half liter of water: one dropper of water-soluble IBA rooting hormone, a very, very small dose of a high-phosphorus fertilizer, and Trichoderma harzianum T-22. That very small fertilizer dose in the first watering of the soil has resulted in success. Water the freshly potted plantlets with this once. After that, the next watering gets no fertilizer, and very light feeding starts with the watering after it. Under a 100 percent humidity dome it is usually at least ten days before they need water again.

chunks.content: Every cabinet and grow area has a light fan to fight fungus and mold. It does not need to be strong: leaves should not be whipping around. The test is slight movement in some leaves, or a little movement in the fabric wall of a grow tent. That is enough to keep the air from going still and stale around the plants, which is what causes fungal problems. When fungus shows up anywhere, airflow is one of the first things to check.
chunks.heading: Every grow area has a light fan running

chunks.content: After planting from tissue culture, leaves sometimes melt away: they turn to mush and die off. This is pretty common. As long as the base of the plant is fine (the base, not a leaf's stalk), keep taking care of it. If leaves are turning to mush, consider a slight change to watering, because you might be overwatering, and add some daily airflow if you can. Early in the stage, even opening the dome slightly for a few minutes gets fresh air in.
chunks.heading: Leaves melting away after planting is common

chunks.content: First: overdoing the start. chunks.content: Any premixed potting soil or similar product should be treated for fungus gnats immediately on first use, before an infestation starts. The method: soak Mosquito Bits (the brand) in the water you are about to water with for a few hours, then water with it. This kills the larvae in the soil far more efficiently than the usual published methods like spraying oil on the surface or covering the top of the soil.
chunks.heading: Fungus gnats: treat premixed soil the day you use it

chunks.content: Past the first mix, plants move to a chunky aroid soil: coco coir, perlite, charcoal, coconut husk chips, and a bit of orchid bark. Monstera and Anthurium both love airflow around the roots; Monstera get the chunkiest version, and Anthurium a slightly less chunky one because their roots start thinner. Alocasia and Philodendron get the same ingredients with slightly more fine material and coco coir to hold water, because their finer roots struggle in a mix that is too chunky. A very large Alocasia with thick roots can eventually move to a chunkier mix, but that is far in the future.
chunks.heading: Second-stage mix after acclimation: chunky aroid soil

answer: Start the dome at 100 percent humidity. Never opening it up from that starting point (or never starting there at all) kills the plant, so don't skip that step. chunks.content: Cut off the affected leaves immediately, even if it is the plant's only leaf, and spray with a copper fungicide. A fungicide can also be applied while watering. If leaf spot keeps recurring, add more airflow to the setup. Isolate the plant if it sits near other Alocasia, and treat the surrounding plants with a fungicide as well, exactly as you would for a pest outbreak.
chunks.heading: Leaf spot on Alocasia: what to do

chunks.content: Big-box labels call tropical aroids medium- or low-light plants. Indoors, they almost never are. These are not outdoor plants unless they are slowly acclimated to sun, but as indoor plants they need more light than people think. Every aroid grown here is treated as a high-light plant with a target DLI of 15 or more, and established plants are given at least 250 PPFD, with 300 or more as the goal. Tissue-culture plantlets start lower, around 150 PPFD (it is not an exact figure), and pick up more light as they grow toward the fixture.
chunks.heading: Aroids are high-light plants, whatever the store label says

chunks.content: Bugs are not common while plantlets are still under the dome, and what to do depends on the bug. Most likely it is springtails or soil mites; if so, leave them, because they are beneficial. A harmful pest such as thrips or spider mites must be treated, along with all the plants around it, but plantlets are extremely fragile at that stage, which puts you in a difficult position. A plantlet cannot be sprayed and then put under grow lights: it will most likely burn and die. Spray gently at night so the leaves can dry off.
chunks.heading: Bugs under the dome: leave springtails, treat pests gently at night

chunks.content: Spider mites are an easier kill than thrips. Neem oil, spinosad, or most other pesticide sprays work, combined with manually wiping the leaves. Wipe both sides of each leaf.
chunks.heading: Spider mites: sprays plus wiping

chunks.content: Thrips adapt to pesticides quickly and lay eggs in the soil, so treatment must be consistent and rotated between different pesticides. When thrips are found, spray every four days, mostly with a spinosad-based pesticide. Where it is legal, systemic granules (imidacloprid or a similar active ingredient) watered into the soil protect the plant for a month or more; the plant takes the chemical up and pests that bite it die. Do not use systemic granules if spider mites are present: they have been found to speed up spider-mite reproduction rather than kill them, so an infestation can spread faster.
chunks.heading: Thrips: rotate sprays every four days, or use systemic granules

chunks.content: The first potting mix for tissue-culture Monstera and Anthurium is tree fern fiber and perlite at about 45 percent each, plus about 10 percent coco coir. For Alocasia and Philodendron it is the same mix with about 20 percent coco coir, with the tree fern and perlite each dropping slightly to make room. The only goal of the change is a bit more dense material for fine roots to pull water from. Any plant with very fine, thin roots gets the denser mix, because fine roots need less airflow and need to be able to grab water from the substrate. A mix that is too dense is one of the most common beginner mistakes.
